title: Single vs. multiple sets of resistance exercise for muscle hypertrophy: a meta-analysis
authors: Krieger JW
journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
design: Meta-analysis using multilevel meta-regression: 55 effect sizes nested within 19 treatment groups and 8 studies, comparing single vs multiple sets per exercise (J Strength Cond Res 2010, Krieger)
population: Adults in resistance-training studies comparing single vs multiple sets per exercise
sample_size: 8 studies, 19 treatment groups, 55 effect sizes (participant total not seen)
what_it_found: Pooling 8 studies, doing multiple sets per exercise gave slightly more muscle growth than doing a single set (effect size difference 0.10, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.19, p = 0.016). Doing 2-3 and 4-6 sets both did better than 1 set but did not differ from each other.
limitations: It has only 8 studies, and it counted volume as sets per exercise per session rather than weekly sets per muscle, so it cannot test the 10- or 20-set thresholds directly.
abstract_quote: The purpose of this study was to use multilevel meta-regression to compare the effects of single and multiple sets per exercise on muscle hypertrophy.
verification_notes: PubMed record for PMID 20300012 matches the title, sole author James W. Krieger, J Strength Cond Res 2010 Apr;24(4):1150-9, and lists the DOI 10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181d4d436, which was missing from the source. The BISp-SURF record confirms the title. The results gave the abstract conclusion as 'multiple sets associated with 40% greater hypertrophy-related ESs than 1 set'. I did not see the specific numbers (0.10 +/- 0.04, CI, p=0.016) in the results. No retraction, erratum or expression of concern was found. There are published critiques (a 2012 critical review in Medicina Sportiva and a 'Beware the Meta-Analysis' commentary), but these are not formal notices. | PubMed record confirmed: title, journal, year and PMID match. The researcher's numbers match the abstract as shown in search results. Caveats: only 8 studies; volume is sets per exercise per session, not weekly sets per muscle, so it does not test the 10 or 20 weekly-set thresholds directly; participant total and training status not seen. No retraction or erratum notice seen. The verifiedQuote is the purpose sentence, because no finding sentence was seen word for word.

title: Dose-response relationship between weekly resistance training volume and increases in muscle mass: A systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Ogborn D, Krieger JW
design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (meta-regression) of 15 studies, 34 treatment groups (J Sports Sci 2017; Schoenfeld, Ogborn, Krieger)
population: Adults in RCTs comparing different weekly resistance-training set volumes, with direct measures of muscle size
sample_size: 15 studies, 34 treatment groups (participant total not seen)
what_it_found: Across 15 studies (34 training groups), each extra weekly set per muscle was linked to about 0.37% more muscle growth (P = 0.002). Higher-volume groups grew about 3.9 percentage points more than lower-volume groups in the same studies.
limitations: Comparing under 5, 5-9 and 10 or more weekly sets showed only a non-significant trend (P = 0.074), so the 10-set cut-off is not backed by a significant category comparison, and it shares an author with Krieger 2010.
abstract_quote: Each additional set was associated with an increase in effect size (ES) of 0.023
verification_notes: PubMed PMID 27433992 matches: Schoenfeld, Ogborn, Krieger, J Sports Sci 2017 Jun;35(11):1073-1082, epub 19 Jul 2016, DOI 10.1080/02640414.2016.1210197 (missing from the source; added). Year 2017 is the issue year and 2016 the online year, both legitimate. The results confirm 15 studies and 34 treatment groups, and P = 0.002 for weekly sets as a continuous variable. PubMed also lists a comment, 'Reliability of meta-analyses to evaluate resistance training programmes' (PMID 27809704). It is a commentary, not a correction. No retraction, erratum or expression of concern was found. | PubMed record confirmed, and all of the researcher's numbers match the abstract as shown in search results. Caveat for the app: the categorical comparison that matches the '<10 vs 10+' framing was only a non-significant trend (P = 0.074), so the 10-set threshold rests on the continuous dose-response, not on a significant category contrast. The verifiedQuote is a sentence fragment rendered in the search snippet. No retraction or erratum notice seen.

title: A Systematic Review of The Effects of Different Resistance Training Volumes on Muscle Hypertrophy
authors: Baz-Valle E, et al.
design: Systematic review with quantitative synthesis: 7 studies in the qualitative synthesis, 6 in the quantitative. Low-volume groups (<12 weekly sets) were excluded from the quantitative analysis, which compared moderate (12-20) with high (>20) weekly sets in trained men (J Hum Kinet 2022;81:199-210; Baz-Valle, Balsalobre-Fernandez, Alix-Fages, Santos-Concejero)
population: Young resistance-trained men
sample_size: 7 studies in the qualitative synthesis, 6 in the quantitative analysis (participant total not seen)
what_it_found: In 6 studies of trained men, moderate (12-20) and high (more than 20) weekly volumes gave similar growth in the quadriceps (p = 0.19) and biceps (p = 0.59), but high volume did better for the triceps (p = 0.01). The authors suggested 12-20 weekly sets as a standard recommendation for trained men.
limitations: It left low-volume groups out of its pooled analysis, so it cannot speak to raising volume from under 10 sets, and it covers only young trained men.
abstract_quote: no differences between moderate and high training volume responses for the quadriceps (p = 0.19) and the biceps brachii (p = 0.59)
verification_notes: PubMed PMID 35291645 lists PMCID PMC8884877 and DOI 10.2478/hukin-2022-0017, with first author Eneko Baz-Valle, J Hum Kinet 2022. Repository and journal pages confirm vol. 81, pp. 199-210, 7 studies in the qualitative analysis and 6 in the quantitative one, and the 12-20 weekly sets conclusion for young trained men. I did not see the full author list. No retraction, erratum or expression of concern was found. | Identifiers, authors and journal confirmed. The researcher's finding 'no clear extra benefit above 20' leaves out the significant triceps result favouring >20 sets (p = 0.01). Also, low-volume groups were excluded from the quantitative analysis, so this review does not test raising volume from low to moderate, which is the main claim. It bears only on the 'above 20 is uncertain' part, where it is mixed. Population is young resistance-trained men only. The verifiedQuote is a fragment from the search snippet.

title: The Resistance Training Dose Response: Meta-Regressions Exploring the Effects of Weekly Volume and Frequency on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gains
authors: Pelland JC, Remmert JF, Robinson ZP, Hinson SR, Zourdos MC
design: Systematic review with multilevel Bayesian meta-regressions of 67 studies, 2,058 participants, adjusted for intervention duration and training status (Sports Medicine; Pelland, Remmert, Robinson, Hinson, Zourdos; DOI 10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w)
population: Adults in resistance-training studies, adjusted for training status and intervention duration
what_it_found: Pooling 67 studies and 2,058 participants, the authors found a 100% posterior probability that more weekly sets lead to more muscle growth, with each extra set adding less than the one before. Counting indirect sets from compound exercises as a fraction of a set fitted the data best.
limitations: Participants were reported to be mostly untrained or recreationally trained, in studies of about 5-12 weeks, and the study and participant totals were not seen in the verified abstract text.
verification_notes: PubMed PMID 41343037 matches the title: Sports Med Feb 2026;56:481-505, epub 4 Dec 2025, first author Joshua C. Pelland (Florida Atlantic University). A citation listing (sponet) gives the DOI 10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w with authors Pelland, Remmert, Robinson, Hinson, Zourdos and 56(2):481-505, 2026. A second listing gives the online date 2025-12-04. This is the peer-reviewed journal version. The SportRxiv record is an earlier preprint (first posted Oct 2024). The abstract snippet confirms that strength shows more pronounced diminishing returns than hypertrophy. I did not see the 67 studies / 2,058 participants figures or the quoted sentence. No retraction, correction or expression of concern was found. The Sports Medicine notices that came up belong to other papers. | PubMed record confirmed for PMID 41343037 (Sports Medicine, 2026, same authors). The design, n and main findings match the researcher's summary. The researcher's quote was not seen word for word: the search rendering read 'the posterior probability of the marginal slope exceeding zero was 100% for both hypertrophy and strength', which differs in word order. So quoteVerbatim is false and verifiedQuote is null. Volume and page numbers (56(2):481-505) were not seen. Secondary summaries say participants were mostly untrained or recreationally trained and studies lasted 5-12 weeks (not checked against the abstract). No retraction or erratum seen.

title: Resistance training variables for optimization of muscle hypertrophy: an umbrella review
authors: Bernárdez-Vázquez R, Raya-González J, Castillo D, Beato M
journal: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
design: Umbrella review of meta-analyses (PRISMA; PubMed/MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, Web of Science): 14 of 52 meta-analyses included, covering 178 primary studies and 4,784 participants (Front Sports Act Living 2022; DOI 10.3389/fspor.2022.949021; PMC9302196; published as a Mini Review)
population: Healthy adults in resistance-training meta-analyses
sample_size: 14 meta-analyses included (of 52 screened); 9 rated high quality (81-88%), the rest moderate (63-75%)
what_it_found: This review of 14 meta-analyses (178 primary studies, 4,784 participants) concluded that at least 10 sets per muscle group per week is optimal for muscle growth. Light or heavy loads both work when sets are taken to or near failure.
limitations: It pools overlapping meta-analyses, including Schoenfeld 2017, so it is not independent evidence and does not itself test a precise 10-set threshold.
abstract_quote: at least 10 sets per week per muscle group is optimal
verification_notes: There is no PMID in the source, and I did not see one in any result after two searches. The PMID is left unknown and should not be guessed. The DOI 10.3389/fspor.2022.949021 is confirmed on the Frontiers page and in DOAJ (Jul 2022). The paper is in PMC as PMC9302196 (added). Authors are Roberto Bernárdez-Vázquez, Javier Raya-González, Daniel Castillo and Marco Beato. The citation is Front Sports Act Living 2022, vol. 4, article 949021, published 4 Jul 2022. PMC and repository pages confirm 14 of 52 meta-analyses (178 primary studies, 4,784 participants), quality ratings of 81-88% high and 63-75% moderate, and the conclusion of at least 10 sets per week per muscle group. It is in a peer-reviewed journal indexed in PMC/Crossref. No retraction, erratum or expression of concern was found. | Authors, journal, date and DOI confirmed. PMCID PMC9302196 seen; PMID not seen. The quality ratings (9 high at 81-88%, the rest moderate) were not checked in the search output. The article is labelled a Mini Review but uses umbrella-review methods, so I rated the design strong. Its volume conclusion relies on overlapping meta-analyses, including Schoenfeld 2017, so it is not independent evidence. The verifiedQuote is a fragment from the search snippet.

title: Resistance Training Volume Enhances Muscle Hypertrophy but Not Strength in Trained Men
authors: Schoenfeld, Contreras, Krieger, Grgic, Delcastillo, Belliard, Alto
design: Randomised controlled trial: 34 healthy resistance-trained men randomised to 1 set (n=11), 3 sets (n=12) or 5 sets (n=11) per exercise per session, 3 sessions a week for 8 weeks (Med Sci Sports Exerc 2019;51(1):94-103; PMC6303131)
population: Healthy resistance-trained men
what_it_found: In 34 trained men training 3 times a week for 8 weeks, doing 3 or 5 sets per exercise grew the elbow flexors, mid-thigh and lateral thigh more than doing 1 set. Gains in strength and endurance did not differ between the groups.
limitations: It is a small trial in trained men only, shares authors with the Krieger and Schoenfeld meta-analyses, and its top group went well above 20 weekly sets, so it cannot show where gains level off.
abstract_quote: Muscle size increased in most measured sites in all groups, with significant increases favoring the higher-volume conditions for the elbow flexors, mid-thigh, and lateral thigh
verification_notes: The first PMID-only search returned nothing relevant. A title plus PMID search found the PubMed record 30153194, which matches the title, Schoenfeld et al., and Med Sci Sports Exerc 2019 Jan;51(1):94-103. PMC6303131 matches, and DOI 10.1249/MSS.0000000000001764 was seen in the results. The results confirm 34 resistance-trained men in 1, 3 or 5 set groups, 3 sessions a week for 8 weeks, no between-group strength differences, and hypertrophy favouring higher volume at the elbow flexors, mid-thigh and lateral thigh. I did not see the elbow extensor effect sizes. A 'Response' letter appeared in Med Sci Sports Exerc 2019;51(9):1972 (PMID 31415024). It is correspondence, not a correction. No retraction, erratum or expression of concern was found. | Title, journal, citation and PMCID confirmed. PMID 30153194 not directly seen in the search output. The main finding matches the researcher's summary. The elbow extensor effect sizes the researcher cites (0.12, 0.30, 0.55) were NOT seen in any abstract text I could retrieve, so treat them as unverified and remove them unless checked. Note that the high-volume group (5 sets x 3 sessions, roughly 30+ weekly sets per muscle) beat moderate at some sites, so this trial leans towards benefit above 20 sets. That is compatible with 'uncertain', but does not show a plateau.

title: Dose-Response of 1, 3, and 5 Sets of Resistance Exercise on Strength, Local Muscular Endurance, and Hypertrophy
authors: Radaelli R, Fleck SJ, Leite T, Leite RD, Pinto RS, Fernandes L, Simão R
journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
design: Randomised trial: 48 men with no weight-training experience randomised to 1-SET, 3-SET or 5-SET training groups, 3 sessions a week for about 6 months (J Strength Cond Res 2015;29(5):1349-58; Radaelli et al.)
population: Men with no weight-training experience
what_it_found: In 48 untrained men training 3 times a week for about 6 months, elbow flexor thickness rose in the 3-set and 5-set groups, most at 5 sets. Only the 5-set group increased elbow extensor thickness.
limitations: It is a single trial in untrained men only, and a published critical letter about the paper was not reviewed.
abstract_quote: The 3-SET and 5-SET groups significantly increased elbow flexor muscle thickness (MT) with the 5-SET increase being significantly greater than the other 2 training groups (p ≤ 0.05).
verification_notes: The PMID was missing from the source. It is 25546444, the PubMed record for this paper (MEDLINE-indexed per the BVS 'mdl-25546444' record). The results confirm 48 untrained men randomised to 1, 3 or 5 sets or a control group, with training over 6 months, 3 times a week. Only the 3-set and 5-set groups increased elbow flexor thickness, and the 5-set gain was larger. No retraction or expression of concern was found. A 2017 letter, 'Manuscript clarification: Dose-response of 1, 3, and 5 sets...' (Gentil, Fisher, Steele, Arruda; J Strength Cond Res 31(1):e5-e7), is a critical letter to the editor, not an erratum. I did not see its content, so its implications are unverified. | Citation seen on PubMed as a 'similar article' entry (J Strength Cond Res. 2015 May;29(5):1349-58), but no PMID was seen. The abstract came from mirrors (bisp-surf, academia, LWW). The finding matches the researcher's summary. The control group the researcher lists was not confirmed in the text I saw. Untrained men only; the intervention lasted about 6 months. The verifiedQuote is as rendered in the search snippet.

title: Dose-Response Relationship of Weekly Resistance-Training Volume and Frequency on Muscular Adaptations in Trained Men
authors: Heaselgrave SR, Blacker J, Smeuninx B, McKendry J, Breen L
journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
design: Randomised controlled trial (PubMed publication type RCT): 49 resistance-trained men randomised to LOW (n=17; 9 weekly biceps sets, 1 session a week), MOD (n=15; 18 sets, 2 sessions) or HIGH (n=17; 27 sets, 2 sessions) for 6 weeks (Int J Sports Physiol Perform 2019;14(3):360-368)
population: Resistance-trained men
what_it_found: In 49 trained men over 6 weeks, 9 weekly biceps sets increased muscle thickness about as much as 18 or 27 sets, with no statistically significant difference between groups. The higher-volume groups may have gained more strength.
limitations: It is a short trial on one muscle, and the 9-set group also trained less often (once a week against twice), so the effect of volume cannot be separated from frequency.
abstract_quote: 9 weekly sets of biceps-focused RT, performed in 1 weekly session, are sufficient to increase MT
verification_notes: PubMed PMID 30160627 matches the title: Int J Sports Physiol Perform 2019;14(3):360-368, DOI 10.1123/ijspp.2018-0427. Authors are Samuel R. Heaselgrave, Joe Blacker, Benoit Smeuninx, James McKendry and Leigh Breen. The University of Birmingham repository (accepted manuscript, accepted 13 Aug 2018) confirms the DOI. Its title says 'Trained Males' instead of 'Trained Men', which is a manuscript-version wording difference. The results confirm 49 trained males randomised to low, moderate or high weekly volume. The conclusion is that 9 weekly sets in one session increased biceps thickness, and 18-27 sets over 2 sessions may give greater strength gains. No retraction, erratum or expression of concern was found. | PubMed record confirmed (PMID, DOI, n, group sizes, design). The hypertrophy outcome is null between groups. It does not support 'more sets leads to more growth', and it runs against raising volume from under 10 to 10 or more weekly sets for biceps in trained men, so I marked findingSupported fail under the null-result rule. The proposed statement does cite it accurately as a caveat, though. The researcher's 'increased significantly in all groups' was not confirmed in the text I saw. The design confounds volume with frequency (LOW trained once a week, MOD/HIGH twice), and the evidence is for one muscle over 6 weeks.

title: Resistance Training Load Effects on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gain: Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis
authors: Lopez P, Radaelli R, Taaffe DR, Newton RU, Galvão DA, Trajano GS, et al.
citation: Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2021 Jun;53(6):1206-1216. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000002585. Corrigendum: Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2022;54(2):370 (PMID 35029596).
design: Systematic review and network meta-analysis (random effects) of 28 studies involving 747 healthy adults. Training was to volitional failure, comparing low-, moderate- and high-load RT. A corrigendum (PMID 35029596) corrected effect sizes for three studies in one figure. The authors say the main findings and conclusions did not change.
population: Healthy adults; only training with sets taken to volitional failure. Load categories: low (>15RM), moderate (9-15RM), high (≤8RM)
what_it_found: A network meta-analysis of 28 studies with 747 healthy adults training to failure. Heavy (8 reps or fewer) and moderate (9-15 reps) loads both improved strength more than light loads, and muscle growth did not differ between loads.
limitations: The verifier did not see the exact effect sizes, including the non-significant heavy-versus-moderate difference, and a corrigendum changed three study effect sizes, though not the conclusions.
abstract_quote: muscle strength improvement was superior for both high-load and moderate-load compared with low-load RT
verification_notes: A PubMed search for PMID 33433148 identified this MSSE 2021 network meta-analysis, 53(6):1206-1216. The PubMed hit was the linked corrigendum record (PMID 35029596), which cites the original. The PMC8126497 page and the Jyvaskyla repository record carry the same title, first author Lopez P and journal. The corrigendum (MSSE 2022;54(2):370) corrected the effect sizes of three studies in Figure 4 (Morton 2016, Jenkins 2017, Ozaki 2018). The overall and best-quality effects changed slightly, but the main findings and conclusions did not change. No retraction or expression of concern was found. The repository abstract shows the quoted conclusion, that hypertrophy is load-independent and strength gains are superior with high loads. | The 28 studies and 747 adults were confirmed verbatim ('Twenty-eight studies involving 747 healthy adults were included'). I confirmed the qualitative strength and hypertrophy findings. I did NOT see the researcher's numbers: high vs low SMD 0.60 (0.38-0.82), moderate vs low 0.34 (0.05-0.62), and high vs moderate about 0.26-0.28, non-significant. They need checking against the abstract or tables. The verifiedQuote is a clause, not a full sentence. I could not confirm the researcher's conclusion quote word for word. One search summary claimed the published wording differs slightly ('seem to be' vs 'appear to be'), so quoteVerbatim is false. The finding that moderate loads also beat low loads supports the researcher's caveat that the edge of heavy over moderate loads is not established.

title: Resistance training prescription for muscle strength and hypertrophy in healthy adults: a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis
authors: Currier BS, Mcleod JC, Banfield L, Beyene J, Welton NJ, D'Souza AC, et al.
citation: Br J Sports Med. 2023 Sep;57(18):1211-1220. Epub 2023 Jul 6.
design: Systematic review with Bayesian network meta-analysis comparing RT prescriptions with non-exercise control. The strength network had 178 studies (n=5097; 45% women). The hypertrophy network had 119 studies (n=3364; 47% women). Br J Sports Med 2023;57(18):1211-1220, PMID 37414459.
population: Healthy adults in randomised trials
sample_size: Strength network: 178 studies, 5,097 participants. Hypertrophy network: 119 studies, 3,364 participants
what_it_found: A Bayesian network meta-analysis of 178 studies (5,097 participants, 45% women) for strength and 119 studies (3,364 participants) for muscle size. Programmes using loads above 80% of 1RM gave the largest strength gains, and all programmes built muscle about equally.
limitations: Loads were compared indirectly through non-exercise control groups, and the analysis was not limited to sets taken to failure.

verification_notes: The PubMed search did not return this paper's own PubMed page. Two other sources tie PMID 37414459 to Currier et al., BJSM 2023;57(18):1211-1220, doi:10.1136/bjsports-2023-106807, Epub 6 Jul 2023: a Google Scholar lookup that carries pmid=37414459, and a PubMed reference listing on PMID 41851754 that cites it. That listing also gave PMCID PMC10579494, and a PMC10579494 page came up in a later search about this paper. I am fairly but not fully confident in the PMCID, because I saw it only through the reference listing and a search hit, not on its own PubMed record. The abstract details match: 178 studies with n=5097 in the strength network, 119 with n=3364 in the hypertrophy network, higher-load (>80% 1RM) prescriptions maximised strength, and hypertrophy was comparable across prescriptions. A search for retraction or correction found no notice. | I did NOT verify the top-ranked prescription SMD of 1.60 (1.38-1.82) or the 'highly robust' threshold analysis. My last search for them was refused because the shared web search budget was used up. I also did not confirm from the abstract that the network was restricted to randomised trials. Comparisons between loads are indirect, run through a common control. Unlike the proposed statement, the analysis is not conditioned on sets taken to failure. title: Influence of resistance training load on measures of skeletal muscle hypertrophy and improvements in maximal strength and neuromuscular task performance: A systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Refalo MC, Hamilton DL, Paval DR, Gallagher IJ, Feros SA, Fyfe JJ
design: Systematic review with meta-analysis of 45 studies (4,713 records identified). It compared higher-load (>60% 1RM or <15RM) with lower-load (<=60% 1RM or >=15RM) RT.
population: Adults; higher load (>60% 1RM or <15RM) vs lower load (≤60% 1RM or ≥15RM)
sample_size: 45 studies (from 4,713 screened records); participant total not seen
what_it_found: A meta-analysis of 45 studies. Higher loads gave larger 1RM gains (effect size 0.34, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.52) and isometric gains (0.41, 0.07 to 0.76). Muscle growth was similar (whole-muscle effect size 0.06, -0.11 to 0.24), and the 1RM advantage was smaller in older adults (0.20 vs 0.34).
limitations: It defined higher load broadly (above 60% of 1RM or fewer than 15 reps), so it cannot confirm the 80% threshold specifically.
verification_notes: The PubMed record for PMID 33874848 matches: Refalo MC et al., J Sports Sci 2021 Aug;39(15):1723-1745, epub 19 Apr 2021, DOI 10.1080/02640414.2021.1898094. The Taylor & Francis page agrees (Vol 39, No 15). The abstract confirms 45 studies (from 4,713), similar hypertrophy (whole-body lean mass P=0.70), and a 1RM advantage for higher load (ES 0.34) that was larger in younger participants. No erratum, correction or retraction was found. The one correction notice in the results was for a different paper (on hypoxia training). | I confirmed the ES values and CIs. I did not see the P values (0.70, 0.47, 0.0003, 0.02) or an explicit statement that the 1RM effect was non-significant in older adults. I only saw that it was smaller (0.20 vs 0.34). I searched for the researcher's quote, but the results paraphrased it and never showed it word for word, so quoteVerbatim is false. Caveat: 'higher load' here means >60% 1RM or <15RM. That is much broader than the proposed statement's >=80% 1RM, so this source supports heavier > lighter in general, not specifically >=80%.

title: Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations Between Low- vs. High-Load Resistance Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Grgic J, Ogborn D, Krieger JW
journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research

verification_notes: The PubMed record for PMID 28834797 matches the title, authors (Schoenfeld BJ, Grgic J, Ogborn D, Krieger JW), journal, year and pages (2017 Dec;31(12):3508-3523), and the DOI 10.1519/JSC.0000000000002200. title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Fiatarone Singh MA, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, Steen JP, Thomas GA, Triplett NT, Washington TA, Werner TJ, Phillips SM
citation: Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2026 Apr 1;58(4):851-872. Epub 2026 Mar 5.
